en: A curse struck the accursed man,
Picking a quarrel with a lion favored by Kydyr,
Faith struck the faith-cursed man.
“Agreed, agreed, agreed,” he said,
Toobalban loomed with outspread limbs.
His leather-flask-like nose bobbing,
Toobalban strutted about.
When he heard the boy's voice,
His heart lay calm as ashes.
“This wretched boy,
Let me seize and dash him to the ground.
God willing, the golden throne,
Let me seize it now.
Let me slaughter him while he is young.
Let me put the wretch to death.
While the boy is young,
Let me sate myself fully on his liver.
The golden throne he sits upon,
Let me seize it now.
The twelve-year-old orphan,
Let me put him to death.
Countless treasures and innumerable livestock,
Let me wrest them from the boy.
The Six Cities and the khan of Kokand,
God willing, just wait,
Let me bring them abundant prizes.”
Thinking these words,
Toobalban stood to face him.
As though he would suck the boy dry,
Toobalban came and stood.
The brave only son left by the lord,
Semetey left by the lord,
Setting these words out clearly,
Made a firm promise:
“By your father's grave, Toobalban,
Make your promise firm.
Swear an oath invoking God.
If in the wrestlers' contest
You manage to throw me,
I shall agree to what you say.
The great gated city of Bukhara,
However many people dwell there,
I shall give them with their cream undisturbed.
If you throw me and go,
I shall proclaim it to my people.
Putting my golden crown on you,
Seating you on the golden throne,
This multitude of Bukhara,
Letting you rule them without their stirring,
The golden throne I mounted yesterday,
Seating you upon that throne,
I shall raise you as khan.
If by chance I throw you,
Without leaving you alive,
I shall offer you as a sacrifice.
If I throw you,
I shall tear apart your ribs,
Pour out your blood like water.
I shall offer you as a sacrifice.
Whether you die or not,
I shall tear out your arm!
Wrestler, I have staked so much livestock;
Will you, wrestler, stake your life?
I have staked my golden throne;
My wrestler, will you stake your life?”
When Semetey said this,
A curse struck the accursed man.
Death drove him, a demon struck him.
“Agreed, agreed, agreed,” he said.
“Agreed, good, hero,” he said.
“If I begrudge you my blood,
May our seven forefathers be unbelievers!”
Looking to either side,
Licking his lips and nose,
Toobalban came up.
When Toobalban came close,
The lord's son Semetey,
Knowing they would wrestle,
“Well done, Toobalban!
I shall agree to what you say.
Whatever may happen, my wrestler,
I shall give you the first turn.
If I do not give you your turn,
Shoeing your white-gray horse,
On the coming Day of Judgment,
Do not disgrace me,
Grabbing my collar to demand your blood-debt.
Take whatever hold you like, wrestler.
Without sparing your skill,
Use it to the utmost against me, wrestler!
If you hold back this time,
“Take your mother eighty times over, wrestler!”
Shouting in anger,
When Toobalban came close,
The lord's son Semetey
Held out his forearm.
The wrestler took his forearm,
Applying all the strength he had.
He was a lion touched by Kydyr.
From Toobalban, his forearm,
He pulled it free without a flinch.
Toobalban held out his forearm.
Now sit and watch
Semetey's fearful might.
He grasped it firmly,
Your terror, son of the Blood-Drinker,
Applied great strength.
Toobalban's forearm,
He took it in a hard grip.
The boy's right limbs,
Did you see how evenly they were formed?
Semetey, born of the destroyer,
Did you see that he was a lion?
Trying to jerk, unable to jerk free,
Toobalban whispered.
Trying to wrench, unable to wrench free,
Toobalban struggled.
Though he died, there would be no regret;
Toobalban did not pull his forearm free.
Struggling this way and that,
Toobalban shuffled about.
Dark blood, a mare-milking's worth,
When your hero gripped hard,
From the tips of his five fingers,
Streamed as though he were pissing.
“Ay-hay! Ay-hay! Ay-hay!” he cried,
Saying nothing else.
He did not heed his cries.
He did not let go of his forearm.
Seized by a fit of rage, unable to stay still,
The offspring of the Blood-Drinker
Gripped him again,
Clamping down firmly once more,
He took a hard grip.
The tongue did not remain silent.
When he gripped again,
The muscles of his forearm,
The farther forearm, the solid bone,
Crumbled into fragments.
The Six Cities, the khan of Kokand,
Andijan behind,
Margalang at the side,
Samarkand before their eyes,
The eight khans who came to the feast,
Their knees bending to the ground,
Pleading for the wrestler's life,
All the beks ran.
Before they could intervene,
Before they could plead for his life,
Semetey, full of anger,
Seized him by the waist and swung him,
With a sharp crack, the wrestler
He dashed to the ground.
The boy unleashed terror.
One of Toobalban's arms,
He tore clean out,
With this, Toobalban
Now lay dead.
The eight khans who came to the feast,
There were dignitaries, there were khans,
All the honored people were there,
There were keen-eared men who knew the news,
Of the adventures of fierce Manas,
There were elders who had seen his ways.
To Kakan Khan's Beijing,
Driving them there, mighty Manas,
Had he not had them slaughtered?
All those old grudge-bearers were there.
They began whispering together,
Speaking words of great mischief,
Trampling the places they walked,
All the khans who came
Of Manas gone to the other world,
Gossiped and spoke ill.
They could not bear to see the boy,
Their thoughts grew ever more wicked.
The ground they trod became a hollow,
They turned staunch enemies of the boy,
Trampling the places they walked,
They prattled and spoke ill.
When the turn of the eight khans came,
Without looking all around,
Without sparing the boy's life at all:
“His father Manas was a hero,
Just such a rash lion was he.
While his khan-father lived,
He used to oppress Kokand,
Beating us, making us cry out,
Six thousand beaver pelts, a thousand ingots,
He used to take as tribute every month.
Unable to bear his tribute,
The Six Cities, Kokand, Margalang,
Used to weep bitterly.
While his father Manas lived,
Throughout the face of the earth,
He used to bring calamity.
Unable to bear his wrath,
Before his khan-father Manas,
Everyone used to weep.
He set fire to the sedge-covered land,
Offspring of the man cursed to burn,
He set the grassland smoldering,
Offspring of the terror,
He poured blood into clear water,
This is the heedless one himself!
In the end the boy will bring no good,
If he lives, he will leave no peace.
Now he has reached the age of twelve;
When he reaches seventeen,
He will never leave us unharmed.
He will not let us turn the plow,
He will not let us dwell upon this earth.
When springtime comes,
He will not let us ride a maned filly.
When autumn comes,
He will not let us eat a fat-tailed lamb.
He will not let us fit the yoke peg,
He will not let us plow in spring.
He will not let us break the earth,
He will not let us scatter a double handful of seed.
He will not let us turn the plow,
He will not let us dwell in this land.
He will plunder our precious goods.
If this orphan lives,
He will wreak great mischief.
Whoever opposes him,
Seizing them, the wretched orphan
Will offer them as a sacrifice.
He will scatter the four kinds of livestock.
This orphan, the lord's son,
Will raid and take the mares.
If we happen to come near,
He will strike our brains in all directions!
Better that upon Bukhara
We bring a cunning scheme.
Deceiving them into agreement,
Better that we ask for the orphan,
And take him as a hostage.
Margalang, midway in the land,
Let us somehow ask to take him there.
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
Gathering swaying girls,
Adorned hips and broad braid ornaments,
Gathering lovely craftswomen,
Their waists a handspan, their faces moonlike,
Let us gather the distinguished ones.
If the boy wishes to take them,
Let us marry five to him.
After doing this for the boy,
The millet beer poured into the wooden vat,
Let it ferment, you fools.
There is a potent poisonous drug mixed in.
Make it stronger, eight khans.
The millet beer poured into the leather bucket,
Mix into it without stint,
That burning poison.
